definition: The contact hypothesis is the idea that contact between members of different social groups, especially positive direct face-to-face interaction, can influence and often reduce intergroup prejudice. Research on it has also expanded to include indirect or vicarious, negative, and online forms of contact, which can relate to prejudice in their own ways.

reasons: The definition states that contact “can … often reduce intergroup prejudice,” but the packet only says research “prioritized the role of positive, direct, face-to-face interactions in shaping intergroup prejudices” and that these had a “comparatively stronger relationship with prejudice,” without explicitly stating that the effect is to reduce prejudice.

The packet supports that the contact hypothesis has traditionally emphasized positive, direct face-to-face contact and has recently expanded to indirect/vicarious, negative, and online contact, but it does not explicitly support the claim that contact often reduces prejudice.

The wording broadens the source beyond what is stated by adding a general causal claim about reducing prejudice; the packet only reports associations and comparative relationships in two studies, not a general clinical or empirical consensus.
